name: Murik
confidence_why: Abbott 1985, the only phonological description of Murik and the source behind Hayes 1995 and StressTyp2, states that each word carries one stress, on the first long vowel or else on the initial syllable, and the hedge in the record is Abbott's own: on the strength of six words and one minimal pair he leaves open whether long vowels attract stress or stress lengthens the vowel.

new_statements.quote: p. 346: "Within this corpus of data all phonological words feature simple nuclei composed of a single syllable and a single unit of stress. [...] Concerning the unit of stress within the nucleus of the phonological word and the feature of length found within the corpus of data used for this analysis, stress is predictable as occurring on the first lengthened vowel or, if there are no long vowels, then word initially." p. 342: "The phonological word is defined by an optional pre-tonic slot filled by one to three syllables; an obligatory tonic slot, the simple nucleus, filled by one stressed syllable; and an optional post-tonic slot filled by one to six syllables. However, the maximum number of syllables is seven."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Murik (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so this fills the record rather than contradicting it: stress is culminative (one per word), attracted to the first long vowel and otherwise initial, i.e. a weight-sensitive default-to-initial system in Abbott's explicit statement, with the caveat that his preferred analysis derives length from stress and so treats stress position as contrastive. Not in the works list; the listed 1978 grammar is not available online.
new_statements.rule_in_words: One stress per phonological word. Stress falls on the first long (lengthened) vowel of the word; if the word has no long vowel, stress is word-initial. The stressed syllable may be preceded by up to three pre-tonic syllables and followed by up to six post-tonic syllables, so stress can sit on any of syllables 1-4 depending on where the first long vowel is (e.g. ['damag] 'garden', [ga'i.n] 'canoe', [anənpha'rɛ.th] 'lightning'). Abbott notes, however, that his most efficient analysis treats vowel length as derived from stress on non-initial syllables (p. 347), which makes the placement of the single stress lexically contrastive rather than length-driven; he leaves two alternatives open (stress phonemic / length derived, or underlying double vowels attracting stress).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: 'only one unit of stress per phonological word' (p. 347); no secondary stress is mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 347: six words have a word-initial syllable that is both lengthened and stressed, contradicting the allophonic length statement, and one minimal pair contrasts a short stressed initial with a long stressed initial: ['sar] 'stomach' vs ['sa·r] 'type of shark'. Abbott gives two analyses: (1) stress is phonemic and length derived, with two contrastive degrees of stress intensity word-initially; (2) underlying double vowels are realised long only under stress, with stress on the first long vowel or else the first syllable. Orthography proposal p. 362: 'Stress will be written on the lengthened syllables only, by a small diacritic above the line.'
new_statements.identity_note: Abbott 1985 describes Murik of the Sepik River mouth (Murik Lakes), Papua New Guinea, ISO mtf, from tape-recorded data checked with several informants; no dialect is named. The SIL archive record for the 1978 grammar lists the co-author as Jo Deanne Abbott (the target citation says Doris Abbott) and notes a handwritten query that the date may be 1979.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources: only one source could be read. Within Abbott 1985 itself there is an internal tension the author flags: he states stress as predictable from length (first long vowel, else initial; p. 346) but then says the most efficient analysis derives length from stress on non-initial syllables (p. 347), which would make the position of the single stress lexically contrastive; six words with lengthened stressed initial syllables and the minimal pair ['sar] 'stomach' / ['sa·r] 'shark' are left as unresolved evidence for either 'stress phonemic, length derived' or 'underlying double vowels attract stress'. The listed Abbott & Abbott 1978 grammar could not be opened (not available online per the SIL archive record), so it neither confirms nor conflicts.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding quotation, the phonological-word template and the Level 5 length rule are all verbatim in the Abbott 1985 PDF we hold/txt at the stated pages (346-347, 342, 352). Deciding source: a 1985 Pacific Linguistics phonology article (35 pp) by the SIL fieldworker, the only phonology of Murik in Glottolog's 22-item bibliography; StressTyp2/Hayes 1995 are downstream of it. The classification 'weight-hedged' (stress on first long vowel else initial, one stress per word, with the hedge that Abbott's preferred analysis makes length derived from stress and marks stress orthographically) matches the source's own stated indeterminacy, so no reclassification is indicated. Not 'well-sourced' because the source is explicitly tentative and no later dedicated description exists to confirm it; not 'at-risk' because nothing found contradicts it. Best candidate for improvement is Foley 2018 (paywalled area
